publication_type: Topic-level evidence synthesis combining peer-reviewed articles, a systematic review, district-scale field studies, IoT system papers, and official technical guidance.
country_and_climate: Evidence spans temperate-cold northeastern United States (Boston Public Schools), maritime Ireland, Mediterranean Italy and Portugal, and mixed European school settings. The climate signal is important because winter heating seasons, shoulder seasons, and hot periods strongly affect outdoor-air use, window-opening behavior, and indoor-outdoor CO2 differentials.
objective_and_research_question: The shared objective across the literature is to use indoor CO2 as an occupancy-linked indicator of ventilation adequacy, classroom air renewal, and sometimes airborne infection risk management, while avoiding the common error of treating CO2 as a complete indoor air quality metric. For an IoT classroom deployment, the practical question is how to measure true CO2 continuously, position sensors defensibly, infer when air renewal is insufficient, and turn those signals into classroom-level or district-level actions.
study_design: The evidence base is mixed: systematic review, observational classroom monitoring, district-wide longitudinal monitoring, IoT system design papers, and applied analytics for air-exchange estimation. Most classroom studies are non-randomized field studies with repeated measurements under real occupancy and real operation of windows, doors, and HVAC.
educational_context: The dominant context is K-12 classrooms and primary schools, with some higher-education classrooms used for method development. Ventilation modes include natural ventilation, mixed-mode rooms, and central mechanical systems; continuous CO2 monitoring is most informative in densely occupied classrooms where occupancy varies by lesson and the ability to increase outdoor air is operationally constrained.
sample_and_duration: The strongest large-scale field evidence is the Boston Public Schools dataset, which used 3,659 commercial IAQ monitors in 125 school buildings during the 2022-2023 school year and analyzed 245 million CO2 measurements. Complementary evidence includes a 125-study systematic review of naturally ventilated primary schools and several single-school or multi-classroom deployments with minute-scale or short-interval logging across weeks to months.
environmental_variables: Core measured variables are indoor CO2 concentration in ppm, outdoor CO2 when available, air temperature in degrees Celsius, relative humidity in percent, and sometimes PM, CO, VOC-related indicators, and occupancy context. The most useful classroom ventilation indicators are indoor CO2, excess CO2 above outdoor baseline, daily peak CO2, time above operational thresholds, and decay or recovery behavior after occupancy.
outdoor_conditions_and_baseline: Outdoor CO2 and weather matter because classroom interpretation should use indoor-outdoor difference rather than indoor concentration alone whenever possible. Outdoor baseline also changes over time, and window opening, infiltration, wind, traffic-adjacent pollution, and extreme weather events can alter both ventilation effectiveness and the trade-off between fresh air and outdoor pollutant ingress.
occupancy_and_activity: CO2 in classrooms is dominated by human respiration, so occupancy density, class schedule, student age, lesson duration, room volume, vocal activity, and turnover between classes directly shape the signal. Short crowded periods can create fast rises, while lunch breaks, class changes, and after-school vacancy create the conditions needed for decay analysis and ventilation-rate estimation.
ventilation_and_filtration_operation: Window and door opening, central HVAC outdoor-air delivery, exhaust operation, and demand-controlled ventilation shape indoor CO2 trajectories. The literature consistently shows lower and more stable CO2 in buildings with central mechanical ventilation; filtration can reduce particles and infection risk but does not remove CO2, so air cleaners are not substitutes for outdoor-air renewal when the problem is excess CO2.
spatial_granularity: Room-level sensing is preferred because within-school and between-classroom heterogeneity is large. District-scale evidence shows that building averages can hide important classroom outliers, so one sensor per regularly occupied classroom is the defensible minimum for operational decision-making, with additional sensors only when the room is very large, unusually shaped, or known to stratify.
sensor_specification: Recommended true-CO2 sensor class: NDIR or photoacoustic NDIR. Practical low-cost examples are Sensirion SCD41 (specified 400-5,000 ppm range on its main catalog page, small SMD format, low-power single-shot option) and Senseair Sunrise (NDIR, 0-10,000 ppm, accuracy about plus or minus 30 ppm plus 3 percent of reading, 30 s response, I2C/UART). These are suitable for embedded IoT nodes; higher-power modules such as Senseair S8 or K30 are also viable when mains power is available. For ventilation studies, sensor selection should favor stable true CO2 measurement over convenience features.
calibration_and_qaqc: ASHRAE and EPA both emphasize that sensor performance, placement, and calibration determine whether the data are interpretable. A practical QA/QC workflow is pre-deployment co-location, clock synchronization, documented warm-up behavior, outdoor-background checks, periodic side-by-side rechecks, review of implausible flat lines or spikes, and explicit management of auto-baseline-correction behavior so a sensor is not silently forced toward a false baseline in persistently occupied rooms.
acquisition_and_data_quality: Continuous logging at 1 to 5 minute intervals is usually adequate for dashboards and ventilation management, while 1 minute or finer resolution is preferable for decay modeling and event diagnosis. Data cleaning should remove startup transients, obvious communication gaps, and artifacts caused by unplugging, tampering, or relocation; completeness, uptime, and event annotation are as important as raw accuracy in school operations.
sensor_lifecycle: [uncertain] Field life is multi-year for mainstream NDIR modules, but actual drift, fouling, and failure rates vary by enclosure design, dust, power quality, and maintenance discipline. Battery operation is possible for ultra-low-power sensors, yet dense classroom monitoring is usually operationally easier on mains power because Wi-Fi or frequent uplinks dominate energy use more than the sensing element itself.
recommended_sensor_by_variable: For CO2 and air-renewal work, recommend true CO2 by NDIR or photoacoustic NDIR as the primary variable. A robust low-cost stack is: true CO2 module (SCD41 or Sunrise), separate temperature and humidity sensor if thermal correction or comfort co-analysis is needed, and optional occupancy metadata from schedule integration rather than inferred occupancy alone. Avoid choosing an eCO2-only module for ventilation control or standards-related decisions.
useful_output_and_units: The useful outputs are indoor CO2 in ppm, outdoor CO2 in ppm when measured, excess CO2 above outdoor baseline in ppm, time-above-threshold metrics in minutes or percent of occupied time, peak CO2 in ppm, and estimated air exchange rate in air changes per hour when the study design supports it.
direct_measurement_or_proxy: Indoor CO2 from NDIR or photoacoustic NDIR is a direct physical measurement of CO2 concentration. Ventilation adequacy, rebreathed fraction, occupancy, and infection-risk implications are derived proxies. eCO2 from MOS or VOC sensors is not direct CO2; it is a modeled estimate derived from gas-response patterns and should not be treated as interchangeable with true CO2.
measurement_principle_and_selectivity: True classroom CO2 sensing should use NDIR or photoacoustic NDIR because these principles are selective to CO2 and widely used in building and IAQ applications. MOS/VOC devices such as the Sensirion SGP30 report TVOC and CO2eq-like outputs, which are useful for broad air-quality indication but are not selective enough for defensible ventilation-rate inference or school ventilation control.
useful_range_and_real_performance: The operationally important classroom range is roughly outdoor background to 2,000 ppm, but sensors should tolerate occasional peaks far above that. District-scale evidence from Boston found an average school-day CO2 concentration of 841 ppm with daily peaks as high as 5,080 ppm, so classroom programs should not choose a sensor that saturates near 2,000 ppm if they expect diagnostic use during under-ventilated periods.
operating_regime: Continuous monitoring is preferable to spot checks. A 1 minute interval supports near-real-time alerts and ventilation diagnostics; 5 minute intervals are acceptable for routine dashboards. Warm-up requirements must be respected, and continuous mains-powered operation with buffered local storage is preferable when the goal is defensible school operations data rather than personal portable monitoring.
interferences_and_confounders: Major confounders are poor placement near supply diffusers, returns, windows, doors, corners, direct breath plumes, or teacher stations; stratification in large rooms; changing outdoor baseline; occupancy misclassification; and automatic baseline correction in spaces that rarely reach outdoor-like concentrations. Interpretation is also confounded when users assume that high CO2 automatically identifies every IAQ hazard, which ASHRAE explicitly rejects.
affordable_validation_protocol: For a TCC-scale protocol, co-locate all candidate classroom nodes together with one better reference-grade or better-characterized NDIR monitor for 7 to 14 days under real indoor conditions, then repeat an outdoor-background check at low-occupancy times. After installation, run at least one occupied-to-unoccupied decay test per classroom, document windows and HVAC state, and compare slopes across nodes. Keep photos, installation height, room geometry, and event logs so corrections remain reproducible.
validation_metrics: Minimum metrics are bias in ppm, MAE, RMSE, slope and intercept versus the reference, inter-sensor correlation, uptime, missing-data fraction, and false-alert frequency. If air-exchange modeling is used, also report uncertainty of estimated ACH, sensitivity to occupancy assumptions, and repeatability of decay estimates across days.
installation_and_enclosure: EPA guidance supports placement near the breathing zone, about 3 to 6 ft above the floor. In classrooms, place the node away from windows, doors, HVAC inlets/outlets, corners, and direct solar gain; use a vented enclosure with free airflow; and physically isolate the sensing cavity from MCU heat sources when possible. If the ESP32 or power regulator warms the enclosure, temperature compensation may remain biased even when CO2 is stable.
hardware_integration: Low-cost integration is straightforward with ESP32-class MCUs. SCD41 uses I2C; Sunrise supports I2C and UART; local buffering on flash or SD is useful for network outages; and a 5 V USB or DC wall supply is usually simpler than batteries for always-on school deployments. If LoRaWAN is used, edge aggregation can reduce bandwidth and preserve battery life, but Wi-Fi is simpler where campus infrastructure already exists.
total_implementation_cost: [uncertain] As of August 11, 2026, low-volume parts pricing is roughly USD 22.39 for an SCD41 and USD 5.76 for an SHT45 at DigiKey, while Senseair-class NDIR modules are usually higher. A practical classroom node using ESP32, true CO2 sensing, enclosure, PCB, power supply, and mounting hardware is typically around USD 35 to USD 80 per room before labor, calibration services, dashboards, and ongoing maintenance.
evidence_maturity: Evidence maturity is high for the value of continuous true-CO2 monitoring as an operational ventilation indicator, moderate for low-cost sensor deployment methods in classrooms, and moderate for estimating classroom air-exchange rates from commercial sensor data. Evidence is weaker for universal threshold setting and for strong causal claims that common indoor CO2 levels alone directly drive health or learning effects independent of co-varying pollutants and thermal conditions.
variable_specific_cautions: Do not confuse true CO2 with eCO2 or CO2eq. Do not treat CO2 as a full IAQ score. Do not assume portable HEPA units will lower CO2. Be careful with auto-baseline correction in rooms that stay occupied most of the day. Thresholds should be operational aids, not universal health limits, and any attempt to estimate infection risk or ACH from CO2 must state assumptions about occupancy, mixing, and outdoor baseline.
system_architecture: A defensible architecture is classroom node to campus network to time-series database to dashboard and alerting layer. At room level, the node measures true CO2 continuously; at building or district level, dashboards rank classrooms by peak CO2, duration above action bands, and persistence of poor recovery. More advanced systems add outdoor nodes, edge filtering, and analytics for air-exchange estimation or prioritized maintenance tickets.
connectivity_and_protocols: Wi-Fi plus MQTT or HTTPS is the simplest pattern when school networking is available. LoRaWAN is attractive for district-scale retrofits because it lowers power use and extends range, and the Smart Healthy Schools literature explicitly highlights LoRaWAN for multi-room deployment. The best protocol choice depends more on campus infrastructure, security policy, and maintenance capacity than on sensing physics.
interoperability_and_data_model: Interoperable outputs should at minimum include timestamp, room ID, sensor ID, CO2 ppm, temperature, relative humidity, occupancy status if known, and QA flags. JSON over MQTT or HTTP is sufficient for a TCC prototype; if long-term institutional integration is expected, room metadata and event logs should map cleanly to BMS, CMMS, or district dashboards so high-CO2 rooms can trigger work orders rather than just produce graphs.
cybersecurity_privacy_and_ethics: CO2 monitoring is lower privacy risk than camera-based occupancy sensing, but room-level dashboards can still expose patterns of use, operational failures, or inequities between schools. Apply network segmentation, authenticated brokers or APIs, device identity management, encrypted transport, minimal personal data collection, and governance on who can view room-level results. If occupancy is inferred or linked to schedules, avoid creating individual-level surveillance interpretations.
analytical_methods: Common analyses include descriptive time series, occupied-period summaries, peak detection, duration-above-threshold metrics, indoor-outdoor differential analysis, clustering of classrooms by exposure profile, decay-based ACH estimation, and more recently machine-learning workflows that automate data cleaning and large-scale air-exchange estimation. For school operations, simple and explainable metrics usually outperform opaque models in usability.
derived_index_or_model: Key derived quantities are excess CO2 above outdoor baseline, rebreathed fraction, and estimated air exchange rate. At a practical level, excess CO2 supports ventilation screening, while decay after occupancy or machine-learning workflows based on long sensor histories can estimate ACH. These models are useful only when assumptions about occupancy generation rate, mixing, and sensor quality are made explicit.
decision_rules_and_standards: ASHRAE does not endorse a single universal indoor CO2 limit for overall IAQ, so operational rules should be framed as action bands rather than health-based absolutes. A practical school rule set is: prioritize classrooms with repeated occupied-period peaks above about 1,000 ppm, urgent review when levels repeatedly exceed about 1,500 ppm, and diagnostic follow-up when recovery after vacancy is slow. Any band should also consider outdoor CO2, room schedule, and whether the room is naturally or mechanically ventilated.
intervention_and_automation: Interventions include opening windows and doors, increasing outdoor-air fraction, extending purge periods before occupancy, repairing or rebalancing fans, reducing crowding in persistently high-CO2 rooms, and using dashboards to prioritize HVAC investment. Automation can be as simple as room traffic-light alerts or as advanced as multi-room LoRa-based signaling and centralized control logic tied to ventilation equipment.
environmental_outcomes: The clearest outcome is better visibility of under-ventilated classrooms and faster identification of rooms needing operational or capital action. Continuous monitoring supports reduced duration of excess CO2, more targeted ventilation corrections, and more defensible balancing of air renewal against thermal-energy penalties.
health_and_learning_outcomes: Field evidence links high classroom CO2 with poor ventilation and with worse perceived air quality, nonspecific symptoms, and poorer schoolwork outcomes in some studies, but ASHRAE states that direct evidence for pure-CO2 effects at commonly observed indoor concentrations remains inconsistent. The safer interpretation is that CO2 is a useful marker of occupancy-linked under-ventilation that may co-occur with exposures relevant to health and learning.
objective_subjective_integration: Several studies pair monitoring with teacher or occupant perception and show that perceptions do not always match measured conditions. For classroom management, short teacher feedback forms can complement sensor data, but decisions about ventilation upgrades should rely on measured trends rather than perception alone.
quantitative_results: Boston Public Schools reported a school-day average CO2 concentration of 841 ppm with a standard deviation of 405 ppm, and daily peak values up to 5,080 ppm across 3,659 monitors in 125 buildings. The district-scale findings also showed lower and more stable CO2 in buildings with central mechanical ventilation, reinforcing the value of continuous room-level monitoring over occasional spot measurements.
feasibility_and_acceptance: True-CO2 classroom monitoring is technically feasible with low-cost hardware and scales well when installation and QA/QC are standardized. Acceptance is highest when dashboards are simple, alerts are tied to concrete actions, and the program is framed as ventilation support rather than staff surveillance. District partnerships show that the biggest barriers are maintenance workflow, network policy, and interpreting large data volumes, not sensor availability alone.
validity_and_limitations: Limitations include room-to-room heterogeneity, imperfect mixing, missing outdoor baseline, uncertain occupancy generation rates, sensor drift, and threshold over-interpretation. Results from one district or climate do not transfer perfectly to another, and any claim about infection risk, learning, or health must separate what is directly measured from what is inferred through models and assumptions.
contribution_and_research_gaps: The literature now supports a practical classroom-monitoring stack: room-level true CO2 sensing, defensible siting, continuous logging, and action-oriented dashboards. The main gaps are standardized low-cost validation protocols for schools, better guidance on sensor placement in complex classrooms, climate-specific action bands, and stronger evidence connecting continuous monitoring programs to long-term improvements in ventilation, equity, health, and educational outcomes.
